title: Aeetes and the Tasks
subtitle: A king turns power into a trap

main.author: Apollonius Rhodius
main.locator: Argonautica 3, Aeetes sets the trial; Book 3, normalized characters 22216-22948
main.excerpt: Two bulls with feet of bronze I have that pasture on the plain of Ares, breathing forth flame from their jaws; them do I yoke and drive over the stubborn field of Ares, four plough-gates; and quickly cleaving it with the share up to the headland, I cast into the furrows the seed, not the corn of Demeter, but the teeth of a dread serpent that grow up into the fashion of armed men; them I slay at once, cutting them down beneath my spear as they rise against me on all sides. In the morning do I yoke the oxen, and at eventide I cease from the harvesting. And thou, if thou wilt accomplish such deeds as these, on that very day shalt carry off the fleece to the king’s palace; ere that time comes I will not give it, expect it not.

aid.author: Apollonius Rhodius
aid.locator: Argonautica 3, Medea explains the charm; Book 3, normalized characters 56995-57417
aid.excerpt: And at dawn steep this charm in water, strip, and anoint thy body therewith as with oil; and in it there will be boundless prowess and mighty strength, and thou wilt deem thyself a match not for men but for the immortal gods. And besides, let thy spear and shield and sword be sprinkled. Thereupon the spear-heads of the earthborn men shall not pierce thee, nor the flame of the deadly bulls as it rushes forth resistless.

narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Aeetes orders Jason to yoke bronze bulls, plough four fields, and sow serpent's teeth before he will give up the fleece.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “Hephaestus had fashioned in the palace of Cytaean Aeetes. And he wrought for him bulls with feet of bronze, and their mouths were of bronze, and from them they breathed out a terrible flame of fire; moreover he forged a plough of unbending adamant, all in one piece, in payment of thanks to Helios, who”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Medea explains how to use a charm that gives Jason strength and protects him from the bronze spearpoints and the bulls' fire.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: List the task and the help separately. Jason performs the feat, but Medea’s protection and instructions make it possible. Crediting only the visible fighter conceals part of the poem’s causal story.
